turns.text: The previous story examined Gradient Boosting. Now the camera turns to XGBoost and a new question along the same timeline: Why did researchers need XGBoost, and where were the existing methods getting stuck?

Gradient-boosted trees were highly accurate, but large datasets and sparse features exposed systems bottlenecks. XGBoost combined a regularized objective with an engineering design built for scalable parallel and out-of-core learning.

The system uses second-order gradient statistics, regularized tree scoring, sparsity-aware split finding, column blocks, and cache-conscious computation. These choices make boosted trees efficient across machines and data formats.

Experts generally regard XGBoost as the system that made gradient-boosted trees a default high-performance tool for tabular prediction. Its open-source ecosystem and competition success drove broad industrial adoption.
The thread continues with LightGBM, where researchers push the problem one step further.
